title: Product photography for a bookstore
metaTitle: How to photograph books for a shop
excerpt: Photograph books so people can browse, see the staff's taste, and know what to ask. Keep one crop and one background so the grid looks like a single shop.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, setting the crop for a row of book pictures.
caption: Setting the crop before the covers reach the grid. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many pictures does a book need?
faqs.answer: Give a featured book a straight cover shot and a second frame that shows it as an object, with the spine visible. Add a detail only when there is something to ask about, such as a map or a signature. The grid should use the consistent frame, not a one-off poster.

faqs.question: Why do mixed photo crops matter in a bookshop grid?
faqs.answer: Different crops and backgrounds make the row look like several shops. A person scanning covers cannot compare them, and the page looks unfinished. Pick one crop, one background, and one direction of light, and write them down for the next carton.

faqs.question: What should the alt text of a book photo say?
faqs.answer: Name the book and the author, and say what the view is if it is not the cover. A file name does not help someone who cannot see the image. Write the alt text when you export the file, in a column next to the file name.

markdown:
A bookstore product photography set has three jobs: help someone browse, show the staff's taste, and leave room to ask. The pictures are how the shop looks before anyone reads a sentence. If the frames disagree with each other, the shop looks unfinished even when the copy is careful.

Treat the photographs as one series. Same crop, same background, same distance from the object. A bookshop can be warm. It cannot be a pile of unrelated snapshots.

## What each frame has to do

Covers already exist. The publisher printed them. Your job is to photograph the book as an object in this shop, at a size and a crop the grid can repeat. A scan of the jacket is useful in the cart. It is a poor homepage, because a scan has no light, no paper, and no sense that a person chose it.

Give each featured book at least two frames.

- The cover, square to the camera, with the title readable.
- The book as an object: a little thickness, the board, the way it sits on the table you actually use.

A third frame is for the table, not for every title. A small stack, a hand opening to a page you are allowed to show, a paperback next to the hardback if you sell both. That third frame is where taste and the invitation to ask live. Do not shoot it for the whole catalog. Shoot it for the shelf you are standing behind this month.

Leave the plot out of the photograph. The picture cannot summarize the novel, and it should not try, with sticky notes, arrows, or captions burned into the file. Type belongs in the page, where it can be read by someone who cannot see the image.

## One crop, one background

Pick the crop before you pick the props. A consistent crop is what makes twenty books feel like one brand. Mixed crops, some tight on the jacket and some wide enough to include a lamp, make the grid look like three different shops.

Decide the frame in numbers you can repeat. For a cover shot, the book fills most of the square, with an even margin. For the object shot, the book sits in the same corner of the frame every time, so the eye learns where the title will be. Write the margin down. The next person who photographs a delivery should not have to guess it from memory.

The background should be quieter than the cover. A paper, a painted wall, a table you already have. One of those, used again. A marble surface for poetry and a dark wood surface for thrillers is a mood board, not a system. The covers already carry the color. The background's job is to stay still.

Light from the same side, at the same time of day if you can. Shadows that jump from left to right across a row are as disruptive as a new backdrop. You do not need a studio. You need a window you can return to, and a plan for the gray days, even if that plan is "we do not publish new pictures until the light is back."

Color should be honest to the jacket. A heavy grade that makes every book amber will look like a filter, and it will make two printings of the same title disagree. Correct the white balance once, save it, and stop.

## Browse, photographed

Browse is a row of covers a person can scan. That only works when the type on the jacket survives the thumbnail. If you have to zoom to read the author's name, the crop is too wide or the file is too soft.

Shoot straight on for the grid. A dramatic angle is a poster. A poster is fine as one image at the top of a shelf. It is a bad default, because angles change the apparent size of every book and the row stops being comparable.

Include the format when the format is the choice. A paperback and a hardback of the same title should be two pictures if you sell both, labeled in the page, not implied by a clever crop. Thickness is information. Let the spine be visible in the object shot.

New arrivals can share a small mark in type next to the image. Do not stamp "NEW" across the jacket in the photograph. You will want to remove it next month, and you will not want to reshoot.

If the shop tables books face-out, photograph them face-out. If you also have a spine-out section, one picture of that shelf is enough to explain it. Do not crop spines into squares and mix them with covers. The scan breaks.

## Taste is a choice of objects

Staff taste does not require a portrait of the staff. A portrait series is a different project, and a wall of faces ages badly when people leave. Taste, in pictures, is which books share the frame and how they are handled.

A hand can be in the photograph when the hand is doing a shop thing: opening a page, sliding a volume out, setting a signed copy aside. The hand should look like work, not like an advertisement for hands. Keep jewelry and nails quiet unless they are genuinely how this shop looks. The book remains the subject.

Props are where bookshops start storytelling and end up with a costume. A cup, a sprig, a pair of glasses: one of these, sometimes, on the shelf image. Not on every cover. If the prop changes every week, it becomes the brand, and the books become background.

The bookseller sentence lives in the page, beside the picture. The picture can make that sentence believable by showing the same book the sentence names, in the same light as its neighbors. A beautiful isolated photo of a book you are not actually recommending is how the grid starts to lie.

When a book leaves the table, retire the special frame. Keep the plain cover shot if the title is still for sale. The archive and the table are different sets. Mixing last winter's styled photo into this week's row is how a shop looks stuck.

## Room to ask

Some pictures should make a person want a human answer. A signed bookplate, a slightly worn proof, an edition with maps: photograph the detail that prompts the question, and put the ask next to it on the page. The picture does not need to contain the words "ask us."

Do not photograph a laptop showing the contact form. That is a picture of the website, inside the website. Photograph the object the question is about, close enough that the detail is real: the plate, the foldout, the difference between two printings.

If you cannot legally show an interior page, do not show it. The cover, the board, and the bookseller's sentence are enough. A blurred spread that gives away nothing is decoration.

Alt text is part of the photograph's job. The [W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are built so people can perceive the content, which includes a text alternative when an image carries information. A cover needs the title and the author. A detail of a map needs to say it is the map. "IMG_2041" and "book on table" both fail the person who cannot see the file, and they fail the person searching for the title.

Write the alt when you export the files, in a column next to the file name. Doing it later means it will be done badly, or skipped.

## A shot list you can repeat

Keep the list short enough to finish on the day the cartons arrive.

1. Cover, straight on, shared crop, shared background.
2. Object, three-quarter if you use it, same corner of the frame, spine visible.
3. Detail, only when there is a real question: signature, map, unusual binding.
4. One shelf or table frame for the books you are featuring together.

Name the files with the title, not the camera counter. You will reorder the grid, and you will hand the files to someone else. A folder called "final-final" is how the wrong printing goes live.

Reject frames in the same session. Soft focus, a cover you cannot read, a shadow across the title, a background you did not agree, a crop that does not match the guide. Delete them so they cannot be "close enough" on a busy Friday.

If you add a new background, reshoot the row that will sit together. One new linen sheet under one book, dropped into a row of gray paper, is the mixed crop in a different costume. The grid should look like one afternoon, even when the books arrived in different weeks.

Print the crop guide on a card and leave it with the tape and the knife you already use for cartons. The photography is a shop task, like pricing, not a campaign you restage every season.

## When the grid looks unfinished

The unfinished look has a cause. It is rarely "we need a brand film." It is two crops, two backgrounds, or a mix of scans and photographs in the same row.

Check the row as a row. Squint. If one tile shouts because it is tighter, darker, or busier, pull it out and reshoot to the guide, or move it to a story where it is allowed to be the only image. A single large frame at the top of a shelf can be art directed. The tiles under it cannot.

Scans and photographs can both exist. Use scans in the cart and the confirmation, where the jacket must match what will arrive. Use the shop's photographs on the shelf and the book page. Do not interleave them in one grid. The eye reads the difference as a mistake, because it is one.

This discipline is the still version of a shop with a point of view. A florist has the same need for a consistent frame, and a harder catalog, because the goods change every week. That shop is the next problem: [an online shop for a florist](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-florist).
